Kintsugi is a philosophy, it's the concept of highlighting imperfections, visualizing patches and seams on the area to focus on, rather than focusing on missing details.

This art of precious scars is a technique used as a means of analyzing the idea of ​​loss through synthesis and restoration of the destroyed and a metaphor for the possibility of rebirth.
Recovery from destructive events is possible through care and patching, not through hiding the damage, but by accepting a new state of the object or the whole life.
The world is a vase that is endlessly disassembled and sewn together again, continuing to bear traces of each event.

Non-human entities helped us put these vases together. In the beginning, there were vague forms, these were the shards themselves, created in collaboration with Latent Diffusion. Over time, they have grown in detail, drawing their stories more clearly, thanks to Jax Diffusion.

The code that puts everything together was written by Yulikolay, for which he is greatly appreciated.

When exploring new possibilities for a new work, I stumbled across an article on Pulsar map. Created by astronomer Frank Drake and Carl Sagan, this map serves as a galactic address of our solar system for any extra-terrestrial civilization to find using pulsars as signposts. Though chances of any kind of life form intercepting the map are slim, I'm still fascinated both by the possibility of another planetary civilization finding the map (and by extension our Earth), and the thought of using pulsar -- the remaining corpse of ancient massive star -- as universal signposts and landmarks to map the Earth position for any kind of possible civilization. To me there's something so poetic about this; it made me thinks of how small are we, the Humans, compared to those rotating pulsars that we use as mere landmarks to our location...let alone the whole universe. We are just floating stardust after all.

In this piece I use Lissajous curve array with randomized variable to position the stars and generate spline as 'star trails'. The Lissajous array is interpolated with Perlin noise array to make it less smooth and looks more random.

14802.d:
Calligraphy is about formulating letters, not language. 

One of my first exercises as a design student (c. 1967) was learning to letter. Using a nib holding pen and India ink we sat for 5 weeks in class like monks constructing letters in the style of a font called 15th Century Chancery Italic Script. Our final grade was based on how well we hand lettered a paragraph. It was a grueling process that's why I remember it; quite the way to develop an appreciation for the letterforms and type faces. 

This algorithmic artwork is modern cuneiform. It is based on a theory I've developed called "Language of Vision" which in itself is an approach for creating a "plastic" image. The space-frame or background square consists of a subtle paper texture and defines the tablet. A resizable tile (spatial force) forms the boundary for a "stroke." The stroke within the tile element is created by joining two bezier curves. 

An algorithm called "fractions of the whole" is a "form of spatial organization" which divides the picture frame into randomly sized intervals along each axes that form the variable sized tile areas. The stroke is programmed to fit each area. This theory lends itself very nicely to algorithmic art and provides a general framework for generative art.

There is meaning in every image but that meaning comes from your experience and imagination.

Gravity tune is a collection of 512 randomly generated NFTs on the Tezos blockchain!
Each GT (gravity tune) is a random gravity simulator animation with random background music!

In this collection I designed a series of random gravity spots on the screen and random number of particles, these gravity spots pull each other and finally combine and make a bigger and stronger gravity force. After a few combinations, the gravity spot will collapse and push the particles around the space!
Some of the gravity spots are different and may push the particles from one direction to another!

It's amazing how one can depict the gravity force in the universe with some code lines based on physics.
This depiction, just as in the real world, is shown based on each spot's gravity force, direction & velocity vector, and each particle's unique direction angle. The next frame is created based on the previous one.

This is a model simulator of how gravity works in this universe. Not quite accurate but it gives you an idea! The images looked charming, so I decided to make it perfect by working on the sound and color composition.

I used Tone.js to create the music. This library contains some preset synthesized sounds, and I picked a few which went well together and used them randomly, each part of the music uses PolySynth, FMSynth, AMSynth or Synth.
Each track chooses a random Scale and creates the music based on that.

In general, the music consists of four parts:

- Pad; which plays two octaves lower than the tonic note scale to fill the atmosphere.
- Chords; Created based on the track scale and randomly play between 1-3 measures. (each sentence in music is called a measure)
- Motif sound No.1; Plays in the main octave. Rhythm and notes' delay times are selected randomly.
- Motif No.2; Plays one octave lower than No.1, Rhythm and notes' delay times are selected randomly.

After each gravity orb explodes, the music will pause for a moment and restarts playing. Now chords and motifs move an octave either high or low.


Attributes:

Background: Randomly picked from 22 different colors.
Particles: 300-600.
Particles Color: Randomly picked from 17 different colors.
Particles Speed: Shown as percentage.
Gravities Count: 25-125.
Gravity force: Shown as percentage.
Gravities Color: Randomly picked from 17 different colors.
Gravity type: Normal, Repulsion in X or Y axis, Total repulsion.
Music Scale: Selected from F1-F#3 scales in various styles.
Motive No.1 Rhythm: Randomly created from 6-9 character rhythms.
Motive No.2 Rhythm: Randomly created from 6-9 character rhythms.


Rarity:

Particle number: Approx. 1% chance of 100, Approx. 1% chance of 1000.
Gravity type: Approx. 3% chance of X, Approx. 3% chance of Y, Approx. 0.09% chance of Reverse.
Motif rhythm: Rare chance of Equal rhythm of both motifs.

This is definitely the darkest mint I've done for FxHash, or even in general, and matches my mood as I watch my net worth drill to the core of the Earth. NIGHT WORLD is the 2nd part of a trilogy. After PAPER WORLD, a world made of paper collage where it is always daytime, NIGHT WORLD is a world of night illuminated by its golden paint.

With this trilogy I wanted to create a poetic universe presenting a "cardboard" landscape in the manner of a theatrical set. Each part of the trilogy presents differently the same landscape by playing on the material, the colors, the lights, the atmosphere...

In NIGHT WORLD I wanted to play with darkness and light. The gold paint can reflect differently depending on the lighting. The manipulation of a lamp with the mouse adds the feeling of lighting a night scene.

I chose to develop the project entirely in 3D with Threejs in order to benefit from dynamic shadows, lights, and golden reflections. It also allowed me to add animations which accentuate the theatrical aspect already present in the first part.

- Press [p] to export an image to disk (5000x5000)

Add '&animated=false' to the end of the live view URL to not have the animations of the beginning.

As a reminder, here is the concept of each part of the trilogy:

📌 PAPER WORLD ☀️: It’s a world made of paper collage where it is always daytime 🌊 ⛵️ ☀️

📌 NIGHT WORLD 🌙: It's a world where it's always night. It will be drawn with golden on a dark board 🔦 🌲 ✨

📌 NESTED WORLD ☀️ 🌙: This will be the merging of the previous two worlds into the same item. The world of night will appear last the world of paper in a subtle way ✂️ 🌈 ✨

These 3 worlds are consistent with each other, but they were made to stand on their own. I hope you enjoy them. I had a lot of fun building them 🙂

Controls:

F11 -> fullscreen mode (alternatively you should be able to do this from your browser menu)
s -> save a png of the image
1-8 -> set the pixel density and re-render (default is 2, higher means higher resolution final image; the preview image is generated with a value of 5, at 1080x1080px)
m -> toggle mobile/compatibility mode and re-render
w -> re-render with a white background
b -> re-render with a black background
t -> re-render with a transparent background
r -> re-render with a random background

------------------

Everything in this sketch is primarily driven by the use of uniform random noise. Entropy locking refers to a technique used to limit the sampling space of this random noise, artificially constraining it to a restricted set of still totally random values, in an unpredictable way. Specifically, these two lines are used for this in this sketch:

```
if (random_int(1,1000)>997)fxrand=sfc32(...hashes)
if (random_int(1,1000)>997)fxrand=sfc32(...hashes)
```

Basically, if a certain random condition is met (3/1000 odds), the pseudorandom number generator will have its seed reset. The combination of the bog standard technique of controlling randomness via resetting the random seed, and the decision to do it at random, in a way controlled by the random seed, creates interesting recursive structures in the "entropy-space" of the sketch. Sometimes these will be extremely short loops, sometimes they remain unstable and never repeat. Sometimes, they get trapped in a loop, only for something to change in the drawing, reaching some mysterious threshold of difference that causes a new random number to be generated, breaking free from the temporary loop and becoming "more random" again. 

More recursion and self-reference is included throughout the sketch. A recursive "shredding" process is used to render small samples of the image back onto itself, either smaller or larger. A similar technique is used to create the horizontal or vertical "tears" that slice up the screen. These create feed-forward loops where pixel information stored on the screen is used to generate the next change to the image. When the pixel density is high enough (controllable via buttons 1-8 on the keyboard), immense and complicated structures arise in the minute details. An almost fractal-like pattern arises due to the intersection of the recursive nature of these feed-forward loops, and the recursive nature of the seed-loops created by entropy locking. Additionally, the textures are allowed to propagate in an interesting way, due to the use of transparent backgrounds.

Similarly, the color and positioning of the underlying pixelart is also controlled strictly through randomization and self-reference.

The image is rendered in the flat 2D engine, rather than WEBGL, because the weird pixel artifacts it creates (especially at ultra-high resolution) are very satisfying to me visually, even though I don't yet fully understand them.


I HIGHLY encourage you to increase the pixel density, and export an ultra-high render of your output, if you have a PC capable of it.

The One Tezo Drawings project is a variation of the “Desenhos de um Real” project (2006- ). In it, the artist sets the price of his work by making a rational calculation, equating his artistic production with a consumer good detached from the art world .
In this case, the calculation is based on the amount charged per hour of work from the minimum wage in the United States. Thus, a drawing that took X hours to produce (Wt) will have its price fixed at USD 15.00 * Wt divided by the value in Dollars of one Tezo (Dt) at the time of publication. But for the final price to be 1.00 Tez, the total production time value (Wt) will be divided by the number of editions (Ed). Therefore, the number of editions is defined by the following formula: 1.00 Tez = (Wt*15/Dt)/Ed ==> 

Ed=Wt*15/Dt 


For this particular project:
Permutation of 18 almost mirrored layers of drawings inspired by masks from the Inca, Mayan and Aztec civilizations.

This is pencil work, a study on Picasso's sketch lines.  The original flows together so well, that to be the creator of a work of art like this, the entire picture had to have been in his mind already before he drew it, all happening in an instant.

That is what really inspired me was his ability to be so full of ideas, seemingly entire masterpieces never before even imagined likely already in his mind perhaps before he even hit the canvas, a frenzied succession of works giving birth to entire movements of art.

At the same time I try to capture Andy Warhol's idea where he presents the viewer with artwork on a designer's idea grid. In his style final work is not necessarily just the one best image arbitrarily chosen, but the sum of the ideas for the piece, placed on the grid.  The viewer and artist sometimes cannot make up their mind which one they like better, so Warhol decided the artist's final work is the set of all the ideal iterations imagined by the artist.  I increased the complexity of the grid to mark the technological advancements in design tools since the last century.

Special features include: 
  maxPanes - a variable used internally for drawing grids

This is pencil work, a study on Pablo Picasso's sketch lines.  The original flows together so well, that to be the creator of a work of art like this, the entire picture had to have been in his mind already before he drew it, all happening in an instant.

That is what really inspired me was Picasso's ability to be so full of ideas, seemingly entire masterpieces never before even imagined, likely already in his mind perhaps before he even hit the canvas, a frenzied succession of works giving birth to entire movements of art.

At the same time I try to capture Andy Warhol's idea where the artist presents the viewer with multiple images on a designer's idea grid. In his style the final work is not necessarily just the one best image arbitrarily chosen, but the sum of the ideas for the piece, placed on the grid.  The viewer and artist sometimes cannot make up their mind which one they like better, so Warhol decided the artist's final work is the set of all the ideal iterations imagined by the artist.  I increased the complexity of the grid to mark our era, that technological advancements have been made in mathematics-based approaches to design.
